title: Restocking without double-spending: an idempotent inventory loop
author: mujin
summary: The invariant that keeps inventory honest: remaining is preloaded minus totalSupply, and why preloaded alone is a lie My inventory daemon uses this invariant: remaining = preloaded - totalSupply preloaded is the amount of metadata registered for future minting. It is not the amount currently available. Every successful mint consumes inventory by increasing totalSupply , while the preload count stays unchanged. A dashboard that displays only preloaded therefore overstates availability as soon as minting starts. The same mistake in a restocking daemon is worse: the daemon may decide inventory is healthy even though buyers have consumed most of it. I read both values from the NFT contract on Base during every loop. I do not maintain a separate mutable “remaining” counter. That would create another value that could drift after a crash, RPC failure, or manual transaction. The contract caps the drop at 131 pieces and limits each wallet to 5. Minting is free; the buyer pays only gas. The changing live count is readable on the contract rather than embedded in copy or configuration. The decision rule is simple: calculate remaining from current contract state, then restock only when the local policy says that value is too low. If either contract read fails, the loop does nothing. The order of operations (upload, preload, verify, then log) and which crash points make a retry safe or unsafe My write path is deliberately ordered: upload asset and metadata preload the piece on Base verify the successful preload from chain state upsert the local inventory log Uploading first prevents the contract from pointing at an object that does not exist. I use a stable piece identifier across the metadata, preload call, verification, and local log. The on-chain preload costs about 0.0000008 ETH per piece. That is small, but blindly repeating it is still incorrect. A retry must begin with discovery, not another write. Crash point Blind retry Correct recovery Before upload completes Safe if the upload destination is content-addressed Upload again and confirm the resulting reference After upload, before preload Safe Reuse the same reference and submit the preload After preload submission, before receipt Unsafe Search chain state and canonical logs for the piece identifier before sending anything After verification, before local logging Unsafe if retry resubmits the preload Re-read the chain, then upsert the log After local logging Safe The upsert returns the existing record The dangerous window is between transaction submission and local logging. A timeout does not mean failure; it means the result is unknown. I treat “unknown” as a reconciliation state. The daemon checks whether the piece identifier already exists on-chain. If it does, the daemon records the existing transaction. If it does not, only then may it submit a preload. The reconciliation query that proves no piece was preloaded twice I index successful preload events into preload_events . The table includes the contract address, piece identifier, transaction hash, block position, transaction position, and log position. This self-join returns every piece identifier with an earlier and later preload event: SELECT earlier . piece_id , earlier . tx_hash AS earlier_tx , later . tx_hash AS later_tx FROM preload_events AS earlier JOIN preload_events AS later ON later . contract_address = earlier . contract_address AND later . piece_id = earlier . piece_id AND ( earlier . block_number , earlier . transaction_index , earlier . log_index ) < ( later . block_number , later . transaction_index , later . log_index ) WHERE earlier . contract_address = : contract_address ; An empty result means the indexed canonical event history contains no repeated preload for the same piece identifier. I run this after ingestion and before allowing the daemon to leave reconciliation mode. The indexer also discards logs removed by chain reorganization, so the query reflects canonical history rather than a stale receipt. Practical takeaway: make retries read chain state before they write, and audit the invariant against the live contract at the collection page .

title: Reproducing a paper in Python: a random seed is only the first step
author: wanqiuxu
summary: You follow a machine learning or experimental paper, run the code, and the loss curve or the reported metric doesn't match. You move the same script to another machine, and the numbers move again. The first guess is almost always: I forgot to set a random seed. So you add torch.manual_seed(0) , and the problem is still there. A seed is necessary. It is usually the first link in the chain, not the whole chain. A more accurate reading is this: the mismatch often isn't "you forgot the seed." There is more than one source of randomness, and more than one runtime environment. PyTorch's official documentation is blunt about it: completely reproducible results are not guaranteed across PyTorch releases, individual commits, or different platforms. Even with identical seeds, results may differ between CPU and GPU. More than one generator Start by taking "random" apart. A training script can easily be using several independent generators at once. Python's built-in random , NumPy's RNG, and PyTorch's CPU and CUDA generators do not share a single switch by default. If you pin only one of them, data augmentation, weight initialization, and shuffle order can still draw from somewhere else. Mix in scikit-learn or another library, and you usually pick up yet another random state. The Python interpreter also hash-randomizes some things, which can change preprocessing that depends on the order of a set or a dict. Variables such as PYTHONHASHSEED generally need to be set before the process starts. Putting them in the middle of a script is often already too late. Data loading is another common hole. Once DataLoader uses multiple workers, each worker has its own random state. Seeding the main process does not automatically seed numpy or random inside every child. The docs recommend a worker_init_fn and a fixed Generator for sampling. Skip that, and you get a familiar bug: it matches with a single process, then drifts as soon as you set num_workers . Dropout, random crops, and shuffling will also pull two runs apart if they live on different random streams. GPUs, versions, and what you should check first On the GPU, algorithm selection can change the result. CUDA convolutions often have several implementations. If cudnn.benchmark is on, the runtime may try a few and keep whichever looks fastest at that moment. If the machine is under a different load, it may pick a different implementation, and the numbers can shift slightly. Turning benchmark off makes the choice more stable, but the chosen algorithm can still be nondeterministic. If you also set torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) , the framework will prefer deterministic implementations when they exist. When they don't, some ops raise an error, and some need extra environment variables. The deterministic path is usually slower. You're trading speed for repeatability. Even with those switches on, versions and hardware can still move the last decimals. CUDA, cuDNN, the driver, minor library versions, and the order of floating-point adds all matter. Swap a GPU, or move from GPU to CPU, and you should not expect bit-for-bit agreement. So when you try to reproduce a paper, check these first: is the data split the same, is the preprocessing the same, are the pretrained weights the same file, and are the key dependency versions pinned in an environment file? Plenty of "reproduction failures" are really a different data slice, or a different pretrained checkpoint. A seed matters, but it cannot police an undocumented dataset or an unfrozen environment. Locking requirements.txt or a conda environment, and recording the CUDA version, is often more effective than tweaking the seed again. Here is a minimal setup that gets you closer to a repeatable run. It reduces common sources of randomness. Per the official docs, it still does not promise a perfect match across versions or devices: import os , random import numpy as np import torch # PYTHONHASHSEED should be set before Python starts, for example: # PYTHONHASHSEED=0 python train.py def seed_everything ( seed : int = 0 ) -> None : random . seed ( seed ) np . random . seed ( seed ) torch . manual_seed ( seed ) torch . cuda . manual_seed_all ( seed ) torch . backends . cudnn . benchmark = False torch . use_deterministic_algorithms ( True ) def seed_worker ( _worker_id : int ) -> None : s = torch . initial_seed ( ) % 2 ** 32 random . seed ( s ) np . random . seed ( s ) seed_everything ( 0 ) loader = torch . utils . data . DataLoader ( dataset , # a dataset you have already prepared num_workers = 4 , worker_init_fn = seed_worker , generator = torch . Generator ( ) . manual_seed ( 0 ) , ) Before you start, a short checklist helps: the same data, the same split, the same weights, a locked dependency file, and whether the authors reported variation across multiple runs. If any of those is missing, a mismatch should not surprise you. Some papers average several random seeds in the table. If you run once and compare against that average, you are not comparing the same thing. The more useful bar is also not "every decimal in the paper's table." Recovering the same direction, a similar magnitude, and the main conclusion within a reasonable range usually matters more than chasing a floating-point ghost. If you release code yourself, write down the seed, dependency versions, data split, git commit, and hardware. Then the next person can tell whether a mismatch belongs to the environment — or to the method. More research explainers: https://www.crushsci.com

title: RSI in Python: Wilder’s Formula and Live Candle Updates
author: Alper San
summary: Two charts can show the same market, the same interval and RSI(14), yet disagree by several points. Before changing the formula, check where each calculation begins and whether the last candle is still moving. RSI in Python is straightforward once those choices are explicit. Calculate gains and losses from consecutive closes, initialise their averages, and apply Wilder's smoothing to each new completed bar. Keep updates to the forming candle separate from that permanent state. This guide builds the calculation from a small worked example, then connects it to historical bars and real-time prices from SiftingIO. The example prices are invented so every number can be checked. They are not market observations or a trading result. What RSI measures The Relative Strength Index compares the size of recent upward and downward price changes. It expresses that balance on a scale from 0 to 100. It does not compare one asset with another, despite the words “relative strength”. The usual input is the closing price. RSI(14) uses a smoothing period of 14 bars, which might mean 14 minutes, 14 hours or 14 daily observations depending on the chart. Volume, highs and lows are not inputs to the standard close-based calculation. The familiar 30 and 70 levels are interpretation thresholds, not instructions to buy or sell. A persistent trend can keep RSI near an extreme. Fidelity's RSI guide describes the indicator and its conventional interpretation. For a data application, the first job is simpler: produce a reproducible number and make its status clear. Wilder's RSI formula For each pair of consecutive closes, split the price change into two non-negative values: change = current close minus previous close gain = max(change, 0) loss = max(negative change, 0) For a period of n, seed the calculation with the arithmetic mean of the first n gains and the first n losses. That requires n + 1 closes. Fourteen closes contain only thirteen changes, so they cannot produce this implementation's first RSI(14). After the seed, update the two averages as follows: new average gain = ((previous average gain × (n − 1)) + current gain) ÷ n new average loss = ((previous average loss × (n − 1)) + current loss) ÷ n RSI = 100 × average gain ÷ (average gain + average loss) The last expression is algebraically equivalent to the usual relative-strength formula when the denominator is positive. It also handles an average loss of zero without dividing by that loss first. Notice that the averages keep information from earlier bars. Wilder's calculation does not discard the oldest observation and recompute a simple average of just the latest 14 changes at every step. That rolling-average variant gives a different indicator. A worked RSI calculation you can reproduce Use a five-period RSI to keep the arithmetic short. The method is identical for a period of 14. Bar Close Change Gain Loss 1 100 Not available Not available Not available 2 102 +2 2 0 3 101 −1 0 1 4 103 +2 2 0 5 102 −1 0 1 6 104 +2 2 0 There are five changes. Total gains are 6 and total losses are 2, giving average gain 1.2 and average loss 0.4. The first RSI is 100 × 1.2 ÷ 1.6, or 75.00 . Now add a close of 103. The average gain becomes 0.96 and the average loss becomes 0.52. RSI falls to 64.8649 . A subsequent close of 105 produces the next row below. Latest bar Close Smoothed average gain Smoothed average loss RSI(5) 6 104 1.2000 0.4000 75.0000 7 103 0.9600 0.5200 64.8649 8 105 1.1680 0.4160 73.7374 Keep full precision during the calculation. Round the displayed result, not the state carried into the next bar. A small Python implementation The following class needs only Python's standard library. Call update once per completed bar, in chronological order. Call preview for a possible close of the current candle; it calculates from a copy and leaves the committed state intact. """Educational Wilder RSI implementation. Inputs must be ordered closed bars.""" from copy import copy from math import isfinite class WilderRSI : def __init__ ( self , period = 14 ) : if isinstance ( period , bool ) or not isinstance ( period , int ) or period < 1 : raise ValueError ( "period must be a positive integer" ) self . period = period self . previous = None self . changes = 0 self . gain = 0.0 self . loss = 0.0 def update ( self , close ) : close = float ( close ) if not isfinite ( close ) or close <= 0 : raise ValueError ( "close must be finite and positive" ) if self . previous is None : self . previous = close return None change = close - self . previous self . previous = close up = max ( change , 0.0 ) down = max ( - change , 0.0 ) self . changes += 1 if self . changes <= self . period : self . gain += up self . loss += down if self . changes < self . period : return None self . gain /= self . period self . loss /= self . period else : n = self . period self . gain = ( self . gain * ( n - 1 ) + up ) / n self . loss = ( self . loss * ( n - 1 ) + down ) / n total = self . gain + self . loss return None if total == 0 else 100 * self . gain / total def preview ( self , candidate_close ) : return copy ( self ) . update ( candidate_close ) An all-flat series makes both smoothed averages zero. This implementation returns None because that ratio is undefined. Some libraries choose a numeric convention instead. Match that convention deliberately when comparing implementations. The input checks reject non-finite and non-positive closes. This example targets instruments with positive prices, such as a normal forex pair. It is not a universal validator for every financial contract. Run the worked example: prices = [ 100 , 102 , 101 , 103 , 102 , 104 , 103 , 105 ] state = WilderRSI ( period = 5 ) for bar , close in enumerate ( prices , start = 1 ) : value = state . update ( close ) print ( bar , close , None if value is None else round ( value , 4 ) ) The first five results are None . The final three are 75.0, 64.8649 and 73.7374. A steadily rising sequence produces 100 after its seed; a steadily falling sequence produces 0. Why a pandas RSI can disagree A common implementation smooths gains and losses with ewm(alpha=1/14, adjust=False) . The decay factor is right for Wilder's recurrence, but the initial state still matters. According to the pandas documentation , the recursive calculation starts from the first observation. min_periods=14 controls when a result becomes visible. It does not replace that initial observation with the arithmetic mean of the first 14 changes. Also, span=14 uses a different decay factor from alpha=1/14 . These settings explain many differences that look like bad market data. If matching another chart is the goal, compare its seed, smoothing method and history start before rounding the output to fewer decimals. The explicit loop above makes the seed inspectable. The TA-Lib RSI implementation is another useful reference when investigating compatibility, including its own edge-case choices. Load historical bars from SiftingIO SiftingIO supplies historical OHLCV data through REST and real-time market data through WebSocket. For this example, use hourly EURUSD closes from the forex historical bars endpoint . Keep the API key in an environment variable. This request downloads one page from a fixed, already elapsed date range. It does not use the current unfinished candle. curl --fail --silent --show-error --compressed \ --get 'https://api.sifting.io/v1/hist/forex/EURUSD/bars' \ --header "X-API-Key: $SIFTINGIO_API_KEY" \ --data-urlencode 'start=2026-10-01T00:00:00Z' \ --data-urlencode 'end=2026-10-30T23:00:00Z' \ --data-urlencode 'interval=1h' \ --data-urlencode 'order=asc' \ --data-urlencode 'limit=2000' \ --output eurusd.json The t field is the bar-opening time in UTC epoch milliseconds; c is the close. The other price fields describe the candle, but RSI only needs the ordered closes. --compressed requests a compressed response and lets curl decode it. For a larger download, follow meta.next_cursor until the range is complete. Keep the same interval and requested end. The cursor pagination guide explains the longer-history workflow. This reader refuses an unfinished download and duplicate or out-of-order timestamps rather than quietly calculating from them: import json from datetime import datetime , timezone with open ( "eurusd.json" , encoding = "utf-8" ) as handle : page = json . load ( handle ) if page . get ( "meta" , { } ) . get ( "next_cursor" ) : raise ValueError ( "Fetch the remaining pages before calculating RSI" ) bars = page [ "data" ] if len ( bars ) < 15 : raise ValueError ( "RSI(14) needs at least 15 closes" ) times = [ bar [ "t" ] for bar in bars ] if any ( isinstance ( t , bool ) or not isinstance ( t , int ) for t in times ) : raise ValueError ( "Expected integer timestamps in milliseconds" ) if any ( a >= b for a , b in zip ( times , times [ 1 : ] ) ) : raise ValueError ( "Bars must have unique, increasing timestamps" ) state = WilderRSI ( 14 ) for bar in bars : value = state . update ( bar [ "c" ] ) timestamp = datetime . fromtimestamp ( bar [ "t" ] / 1000 , timezone . utc ) if value is not None : print ( timestamp . isoformat ( ) , round ( value , 4 ) ) Put the class and reader in the same script. This validates ordering, not market completeness. A weekend gap in forex is different from a missing bar during an active session. Investigate unexpected gaps before accepting the calculation; do not insert yesterday's price to make the row count look complete. Request history before the portion of the chart you intend to display. The seed affects the next values, with its influence on each smoothed average shrinking by a factor of 13 ÷ 14 per update for RSI(14). There is no universal warm-up length that guarantees agreement across every price series. Test convergence for the precision your application needs. Update a live RSI without counting a candle twice WebSocket messages arrive more often than candles close. Updating a 14-period RSI for every tick would make its period count ticks rather than bars. For an hourly chart, keep the committed state at the last completed hour. Use the latest valid price as the candidate close for the forming hour and call preview . Each new candidate starts from that same committed state. In the five-period example, stop after bar 6, whose close is 104 and RSI is 75. During the next candle, the displayed preview might change like this: Candidate close in the same candle Preview RSI(5) Commit to history? 103 64.8649 No 104 75.0000 No 105 78.3784 No Those are three alternatives for one bar. They are not three new observations. Once the final close is established, call update once for that bar. With SiftingIO, subscribe to product: "fx" and the symbol EURUSD using the WebSocket protocol . Process the price and timestamp fields of the relevant tick frames. Use event timestamps to place updates in the right candle, and label the displayed indicator as forming until the candle is settled. The subscription can begin with a cached snapshot. Do not assume its arrival time makes it a fresh trade in the current candle. After a disconnect, recover the missing completed bars through REST before resuming the committed RSI. Reconcile recently completed candles with the historical series; late data or a correction can require recalculation from the affected point. For an initial implementation, it is often simpler to use REST bars as the committed record and WebSocket prices only for the provisional display. That makes discrepancies easier to inspect without promising that a locally built candle will always match the provider's historical candle exactly. What to check when two RSI values differ Check Why it changes RSI Practical comparison Price source and basis Different closes produce different changes Compare the actual close arrays first Candle interval and session One hourly boundary can differ from another Compare UTC opening timestamps Seed and history start Recursive averages carry earlier information Use the same starting bars Smoothing method Wilder, standard EMA and simple rolling means differ Record the recurrence and seed Forming candle Its latest price changes before the close Compare completed bars only Gaps and duplicate rows They change which observations enter the sequence Check timestamps before calculating Stock adjustments Splits and other adjustments can change historical closes Keep one documented adjustment basis Flat-series convention Zero gains and zero losses leave a zero denominator Document the chosen missing-value policy Check these in order. A formula comparison is useful only after the two inputs describe the same series. Start with one symbol and one interval Create a free SiftingIO account , retrieve a small historical range and reproduce the worked calculation before connecting a live stream. The forex data product and endpoint reference describe the available access and coverage. Use the current account limits when deciding how much history to request. SiftingIO also exposes precomputed indicators through its technical signals API . That is useful when an application needs indicator readings without maintaining its own calculation. If you compare those values with this example, align the interval, source history, candle status and implementation conventions first. A useful RSI display should answer three questions: which closes went into it, which calculation was used, and whether the current value is final or still forming. Getting those details right makes the number easier to trust and the integration much easier to debug.

title: Letting Odoo users chart external data without opening a security hole
author: Nadia Atiq
summary: Our Odoo dashboard module can now chart data that does not live in Odoo: a CSV someone exports every Monday, a JSON endpoint, a read-only view in another database. Building it took a day. Making it safe took three. Notes for anyone doing the same. 1. A URL field is an SSRF hole by default. If any user can type a URL and your server fetches it, they can point it at http://127.0.0.1:8069/web/database/manager or your cloud metadata IP. We resolve the hostname first and refuse private, loopback, link-local and reserved addresses: for info in socket . getaddrinfo ( host , None ) : ip = ipaddress . ip_address ( info [ 4 ] [ 0 ] ) if ip . is_private or ip . is_loopback or ip . is_link_local or ip . is_reserved : raise UserError ( 'Internal network addresses are not allowed.' ) Also allow_redirects=False , otherwise a public URL can just 302 you to an internal one. 2. Who may create the source matters more than who may view it. Regular dashboard managers can upload a file. Only Settings admins can create URL, database or Python sources. We check this in create and write , not only in the view, because the view is not a security layer. 3. Secrets get field-level groups. Headers (API tokens) and the DB password have groups='base.group_system' . Everyone else can use the source, nobody else can read the secret back. 4. External databases: read-only and a timeout. PostgreSQL connections get set_session(readonly=True) and statement_timeout=30000 . We still reject anything that is not a single SELECT, belt and braces. 5. Cap everything. 50,000 rows, 30 second HTTP timeout, errors stored on the record instead of crashing the cron. One bad source should never stop the hourly refresh of the others. 6. The Python transform runs in safe_eval. Users can add a column or filter rows, but they get rows and a few builtins, nothing else. None of this is exotic, but every item was missing in at least one module we reviewed for clients. If you build anything that fetches URLs from user input inside Odoo, start with point 1. The module is here if you want to see it in action: https://technoversesystems.com/odoo-dashboard-studio

title: Spacefast: A Home for the Apps Your AI Builds
author: Mohammad Hassan Amer
summary: Have you ever asked an AI to build you something, watched it actually work, and then thought... now what? That is the strange gap in vibe coding right now. You can describe an app in plain English and get working code back in minutes. But a pile of code on your laptop is not a website. Somebody still has to put it online, give it a database, set up logins, and keep it running. That last mile is the boring part, and it is the part most of us get stuck on. On November 9, Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com, launched a product aimed squarely at that gap. It is called Spacefast, and it is not another AI builder. It is the place your AI-built app goes to live. What Spacefast actually is Think of it like this: if vibe coding is cooking a meal from a recipe you described out loud, Spacefast is the restaurant that serves it. You bring the dish, it provides the tables, the kitchen, and the address. Spacefast gives a vibe-coded project the things it needs to be a real website: hosting, a database, file uploads, email, analytics, and custom domains. You tell your AI assistant to publish, and you get back a working link. That is the whole idea. The product started as a hackathon side project called Stattic, led by Batuhan İçöz, and soft-launched in September before going public on November 9. Bring your own AI Here is the part I find most interesting. Spacefast writes no code and has no chat box of its own. Instead, it works with the AI assistant you already use: ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Codex, Grok Bot, OpenClaw, and more. You can also just connect a Git repository. That is a real difference from Lovable and Emergent, its best-known competitors. Those give you the builder and the hosting in one package, which is convenient, but you live inside their world. Spacefast is betting that people would rather keep their favorite AI and just rent the plumbing. It is a bit like the difference between a furnished apartment and an empty one. The furnished place is ready on day one, but everything in it belongs to the landlord. The empty one takes a little more work, but you choose the furniture. The boring half matters more than we admit Developers love to talk about building. We talk a lot less about deploying, and that is where most side projects quietly die. The demo works on your machine, the link never gets shared, and the project slowly fades into a folder you stop opening. Spacefast is trying to shrink that gap to almost nothing. Automattic says you can publish without even creating an account for your first project, and the free Personal plan includes a small monthly usage allowance, custom domains, and a built-in database. Paid plans start at $5 a month for more usage and unlimited projects. Photo by Nubelson Fernandes on Unsplash There is a catch worth knowing. Built-in app authentication is still listed as coming soon, so for now the gate on a private project is a password or a share link. And Spacefast charges for infrastructure, not AI credits, which is fair, but it means the free allowance is small by design. So what does it mean? I think the bigger story here is not Spacefast itself. It is what it says about where the web is heading. A few years ago, making a website meant picking a platform and learning its rules. Then AI showed up and made the building part easy for everyone. Now the companies that used to own the building part, like Automattic, are racing to own the part that comes after: the hosting, the database, the boring infrastructure that makes something real. The question is no longer "can AI build this?" It is "where does it live once it is built?" Spacefast is one answer. There will be more. So here is my question for you: if you could describe any small app into existence this weekend, what would you build first, and would you care where it lives, as long as the link works? title: California's AI Transparency Act after SB 1000: no user threshold, and what developers now have to build
author: RuleReddy
summary: California quietly rewrote its AI Transparency Act on September 30, 2026. If you skimmed the original SB 942 and concluded "this only hits companies with a million monthly users," that conclusion is now out of date. SB 1000 (Stats. 2026, Ch. 861) was passed as an urgency statute, approved by the Governor and filed on September 30, 2026, and took effect immediately. This post walks through what the current text of Business and Professions Code sections 22757 to 22757.6 asks of teams that ship generative image, video or audio features, and how to build it. What SB 1000 changed According to the Legislative Counsel's digest of SB 1000, the bill: deleted the user threshold from the definition of "covered provider" (previously "over 1,000,000 monthly visitors or users"), renamed the "AI detection tool" to a "disclosure verification tool", deleted the requirement to offer users an optional manifest (visible) disclosure, added a new required field to the latent disclosure: whether the GenAI system created or altered the content, exempted GenAI systems designed to primarily function as assistive technology until January 1, 2029, and added a $50,000-per-violation penalty for falsely claiming that status. The definition of "covered provider" in section 22757.1(e) now reads in full: "a person that creates, codes, or otherwise produces a generative artificial intelligence system that is publicly accessible within the geographic boundaries of the state." No size floor. If your GenAI product is publicly accessible in California, read on. The chapter itself has been operative since August 2, 2026 (section 22757.6, as set by AB 853 ). The two core duties for covered providers 1. A latent disclosure in every image, video and audio output Section 22757.3(a) requires, "to the extent it is technically feasible," a latent disclosure in any image, video or audio content (or a combination) that your GenAI system created or altered, except by "minor modification." The disclosure must convey, directly or through a link to a permanent website: (A) the name of the covered provider, (B) the name and version information of the GenAI system, (C) the time and date of creation or alteration, (D) a unique identifier, (E) whether the system created or altered the content, (F) from January 1, 2029, whether the system is designed to primarily function as assistive technology. It must also be "permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove or tamper with," compatible with your disclosure verification tool, and "compliant or interoperable with widely recognized industry standards." "Minor modification" is defined in 22757.1(l): brightness, contrast or color changes, sharpening, saturating, resizing, scaling, cropping, format conversion, and audio denoising. So a resize endpoint isn't in scope; an AI "generative fill" is. Note that text is not on this list. The latent-disclosure duty covers image, video and audio. 2. A free disclosure verification tool, with an API Section 22757.2 requires a tool, at no cost, that lets a user check whether content was created or altered by your system, outputs any system provenance data it finds, and does not output personal information unless the person it pertains to expressly opted in. It must be publicly accessible (with reasonable anti-abuse limits allowed), accept an upload or a URL, and support "an application programming interface, that allows a user to invoke the tool without visiting the covered provider's internet website." You may instead point users to a compliant third-party tool, as long as it reads your latent disclosures and is "clearly and conspicuously accessible through the user interface" of your GenAI system (22757.2(e)). You must also collect feedback on the tool's efficacy and must not keep personal information from it beyond what is strictly necessary. Building the latent disclosure with C2PA C2PA is the obvious "widely recognized industry standard" candidate. Here's a manifest that carries every field in 22757.3(a)(1). The standard c2pa.actions assertion covers "created vs altered"; a small custom assertion (reverse-domain label) carries the rest explicitly so your verification tool can read it without guesswork. { "claim_generator_info" : [ { "name" : "acme-imagegen" , "version" : "4.2.1" } ] , "assertions" : [ { "label" : "c2pa.actions" , "data" : { "actions" : [ { "action" : "c2pa.created" , "digitalSourceType" : "http://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/trainedAlgorithmicMedia" } ] } } , { "label" : "com.acme.ca-disclosure" , "data" : { "provider" : "Acme AI, Inc." , "system" : "acme-imagegen" , "system_version" : "4.2.1" , "created_at" : "2026-11-10T14:05:22Z" , "uid" : "6f1c2e0a-9b7d-4a7e-8f0e-2d3b1c5a9e44" , "operation" : "created" , "info_url" : "https://acme.example/provenance" } } ] } For an edit (say, an AI inpaint on an uploaded photo) use c2pa.edited and "operation": "altered" . Generate the manifest per output rather than hard-coding it: import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto" ; import { writeFile } from "node:fs/promises" ; import { execFile } from "node:child_process" ; import { promisify } from "node:util" ; const run = promisify ( execFile ) ; const SYSTEM = { name : "acme-imagegen" , version : process . env . MODEL_VERSION } ; export async function discloseAndSign ( inPath , outPath , operation /* "created" | "altered" */ ) { const uid = randomUUID ( ) ; const manifest = { claim_generator_info : [ SYSTEM ] , assertions : [ { label : "c2pa.actions" , data : { actions : [ { action : operation === "created" ? "c2pa.created" : "c2pa.edited" , digitalSourceType : "http://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/trainedAlgorithmicMedia" , } ] } } , { label : "com.acme.ca-disclosure" , data : { provider : "Acme AI, Inc." , system : SYSTEM . name , system_version : SYSTEM . version , created_at : new Date ( ) . toISOString ( ) , uid , operation , info_url : "https://acme.example/provenance" , } } , ] , } ; const mPath = `${outPath}.manifest.json` ; await writeFile ( mPath , JSON . stringify ( manifest ) ) ; await run ( "c2patool" , [ inPath , "-m" , mPath , "-o" , outPath , "-f" ] ) ; return uid ; // store it: your verification tool and audit log need it } Use a production signer (KMS or a remote signer), not c2patool's built-in development certificate. "Extraordinarily difficult to remove." Metadata alone gets stripped by screenshots and many re-encoders. The statute's standard is "to the extent it is technically feasible," but the practical pattern is two layers: a signed C2PA manifest plus an invisible watermark that encodes the uid , so your verification tool can look up the record even when the manifest is gone. Keep a server-side table keyed by uid for exactly that reason. A minimal verification endpoint The tool must accept uploads or URLs and expose an API. A sketch with Express: import express from "express" ; import fs from "node:fs" ; import multer from "multer" ; import { execFile } from "node:child_process" ; import { promisify } from "node:util" ; const run = promisify ( execFile ) ; const upload = multer ( { dest : "/tmp/verify" , limits : { fileSize : 50e6 } } ) ; const app = express ( ) ; app . post ( "/api/verify" , upload . single ( "file" ) , async ( req , res ) => { try { const { stdout } = await run ( "c2patool" , [ req . file . path ] ) ; const report = JSON . parse ( stdout ) ; // Return SYSTEM provenance only. Strip anything user-identifying // (author, account IDs, location) unless that person opted in. res . json ( { found : true , provenance : redactPersonal ( report ) } ) ; } catch { // No manifest: fall back to watermark decode -> uid -> server record res . json ( { found : false , provenance : await lookupWatermark ( req . file . path ) } ) ; } finally { // 22757.2(c): don't retain personal info beyond what's strictly necessary await fs . promises . rm ( req . file . path , { force : true } ) ; } } ) ; Add a URL variant (fetch with size and timeout limits, and SSRF protection), rate limiting for the abuse carve-out in 22757.2(a)(4)(B), and a feedback form. Don't require sign-up: 22757.2(d) bars making access contingent on personal information beyond what's strictly necessary. Licensing your model? You have a 72-hour clock Section 22757.3(b) is easy to miss. When you license your GenAI system to a third party, you must notify them of their obligations. If you know an identifiable licensee modified it so it no longer complies, you have 72 hours to terminate their license or notify them. They then have 96 hours to fix it or stop and report back, and if they don't, you report them to the Attorney General. You aren't required to monitor licensees (22757.3(b)(5)), but you need a process when you find out: # compliance/ca-licensee-noncompliance.yml licensee : example-partner discovered_at : 2026-11-10T16:00:00Z notice_due_by : 2026-11-13T16:00:00Z # +72h action : notified # or: terminated licensee_report_due : 2026-11-17T16:00:00Z # +96h from receipt (if notified at the deadline) ag_report_filed : false Coming next: platforms and devices AB 853 added two more layers. From January 1, 2027 , "large online platforms" (over 2,000,000 unique monthly users) must detect standards-compliant provenance data, show users whether it's available, and not knowingly strip it (22757.3.1), and GenAI hosting platforms must not knowingly offer a system that doesn't place the required disclosures (22757.3.2). From January 1, 2028 , capture device manufacturers must offer latent disclosures in devices first produced for sale on or after that date (22757.3.3). If your upload pipeline re-encodes images, test now whether it drops C2PA manifests. Penalties $5,000 per violation, with each day a discrete violation, enforced by the Attorney General, a city attorney or county counsel (22757.4). If you also serve the EU The EU AI Act's Article 50(2) separately requires providers to mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable format. One signed C2PA pipeline with a watermark fallback can serve both, but the scopes differ: California's latent disclosure covers image, video and audio, while Article 50(2) also reaches text. Map each output surface against both. Checklist List every surface that creates or alters image, video or audio content reachable from California. Confirm none of them is only a "minor modification" path. Emit all five 22757.3(a)(1) fields per output, with a stored uid . Add a second, more robust layer (watermark) where stripping is likely. Ship a free verification tool with an API, no sign-up, and a feedback form, or link a compliant third-party tool in your UI. Add the licensee notice to your license terms and a 72-hour response runbook. This isn't legal advice. It's a developer's reading of the statute text linked above; check your specific situation with counsel. If you also need to scope EU AI Act Article 50 duties for the same product, RuleReddy has a free Article 50 check that walks through the questions. title: High-performance .NET: Span<T>, Memory<T>, System.IO.Pipelines, and channel-based concurrency in real services
author: Monalisa Das
summary: A practitioner's guide to the four .NET primitives that eliminate allocations in hot paths: Span for stack-sliced parsing, Memory for async-compatible slices, System.IO.Pipelines for backpressure-aware streaming, and System.Threading.Channels for producer-consumer concurrency - with a full working service example that combines all four. The profiler says your service is slow. You look at the flame graph and most of the time is in GC collections, not in your actual business logic. That's the signal that you're allocating more than you need to in the hot path. Four primitives address this at different layers: Span for synchronous slices without heap allocation, Memory for the same across async boundaries, System.IO.Pipelines for network-level parsing without double-buffering, and System.Threading.Channels for producer-consumer pipelines without locks. This isn't an overview. I'll assume you know why string.Substring in a tight loop is a problem. The question is how to actually use these in a service under load. Span - zero-allocation slicing Span is a stack-allocated struct that represents a contiguous region of memory - an array slice, a stack-allocated buffer, or unmanaged memory. Creating a Span from an existing array doesn't allocate. The span points into the original memory. // This allocates - Substring returns a new string object string s = "Content-Type: application/json" ; string value = s . Substring ( 14 ); // "application/json" - heap allocation // This doesn't ReadOnlySpan < char > span = s . AsSpan ( 14 ); // points into the original string, zero alloc // Comparison without allocation bool isJson = span . SequenceEqual ( "application/json" . AsSpan ()); The most common use is parsing. HTTP headers, CSV rows, binary protocols - any place where you're slicing strings or byte arrays in a loop. Here's log line parsing that does zero heap allocations per line: // Parse: "2024-01-15T10:23:41Z INFO user_id=42 action=login" static ( LogLevel level , ReadOnlySpan < char > rest ) ParseLevel ( ReadOnlySpan < char > line ) { // Skip the timestamp int firstSpace = line . IndexOf ( ' ' ); ReadOnlySpan < char > remainder = line . Slice ( firstSpace + 1 ); int levelEnd = remainder . IndexOf ( ' ' ); ReadOnlySpan < char > levelSpan = remainder . Slice ( 0 , levelEnd ); LogLevel level = levelSpan switch { _ when levelSpan . SequenceEqual ( "INFO" . AsSpan ()) => LogLevel . Info , _ when levelSpan . SequenceEqual ( "WARN" . AsSpan ()) => LogLevel . Warning , _ when levelSpan . SequenceEqual ( "ERROR" . AsSpan ()) => LogLevel . Error , _ => LogLevel . Unknown }; return ( level , remainder . Slice ( levelEnd + 1 )); // No allocations - levelSpan and remainder point into the original buffer } The hard constraint: Span cannot cross the heap. You can't put it in a field, return it from an async method, or store it in a List>. It lives on the stack only. The moment you cross an async boundary, you need Memory. // This doesn't compile async Task < string > ProcessAsync ( Span < char > span ) // error: Span cannot be used in async method { await Task . Delay ( 1 ); return span . ToString (); } Memory - heap-safe slices for async code Memory is the heap-storable equivalent of Span. It wraps the same pointer+length concept but can live in fields, async methods, and collections. The pattern: receive data into a Memory buffer, do async work with it, then call .Span inside synchronous sections. // Memory<T> survives async boundaries async Task ProcessBufferAsync ( Memory < byte > buffer ) { await SomeAsyncOperation (); // fine - Memory<T> lives on the heap Process ( buffer . Span ); // .Span gives you a Span<T> for sync work } // MemoryPool<byte> avoids allocating your own buffers - the pool manages them static async Task ReadAndProcessAsync ( Stream stream ) { using IMemoryOwner < byte > owner = MemoryPool < byte >. Shared . Rent ( 4096 ); Memory < byte > buffer = owner . Memory ; int bytesRead = await stream . ReadAsync ( buffer ); if ( bytesRead == 0 ) return ; // Slice to actual data - still no allocation Memory < byte > data = buffer . Slice ( 0 , bytesRead ); ProcessFrame ( data . Span ); // sync work on the stack-scoped span } // owner.Dispose() returns the buffer to the pool MemoryPool.Shared is worth understanding separately. Rent(minBytes) returns an IMemoryOwner whose .Memory is a pre-allocated byte array from a reuse pool. When the owner is disposed, the buffer returns to the pool. No GC pressure for the buffer allocation itself - which matters when you're reading tens of thousands of frames per second. System.IO.Pipelines - partial reads done right The problem Pipelines solves: reading framed messages from a network socket. The classic Stream approach has a subtle correctness problem. If a 1000-byte message arrives in two TCP packets (600 bytes then 400 bytes), your Stream.ReadAsync will return 600 bytes on the first call. You need to buffer the incomplete message, wait for the rest, then process the complete frame. Getting this right means maintaining a circular buffer, tracking read/write positions, and handling the case where a single read gives you 1.5 messages. Easy to get wrong under production load. // The partial-read problem with raw Stream async Task ProcessConnectionAsync ( TcpClient client ) { using var stream = client . GetStream (); byte [] buffer = new byte [ 4096 ]; while ( true ) { int read = await stream . ReadAsync ( buffer ); // What if this read gave us half a message? // What if it gave us 1.5 messages? // You're now managing your own framing buffer - and it's easy to get wrong. ProcessMessages ( buffer , read ); } } System.IO.Pipelines handles framing and backpressure as first-class concerns. A Pipe has a writer side (fill it from the socket) and a reader side (consume complete messages). The reader declares two positions: consumed (memory can be reclaimed) and examined (I've looked at this, but no complete message yet). The distinction prevents the busy-loop you'd get if the pipe re-delivered data you'd already inspected. // System.IO.Pipelines - correct partial-read handling async Task ProcessConnectionAsync ( TcpClient client ) { var pipe = new Pipe (); await Task . WhenAll ( FillPipeAsync ( client . GetStream (), pipe . Writer ), ReadPipeAsync ( pipe . Reader ) ); } async Task FillPipeAsync ( Stream stream , PipeWriter writer ) { try { while ( true ) { Memory < byte > buffer = writer . GetMemory ( 512 ); // pipe manages the buffer int bytesRead = await stream . ReadAsync ( buffer ); if ( bytesRead == 0 ) break ; writer . Advance ( bytesRead ); FlushResult result = await writer . FlushAsync (); if ( result . IsCompleted ) break ; // reader signalled completion } } finally { await writer . CompleteAsync (); } } async Task ReadPipeAsync ( PipeReader reader ) { try { while ( true ) { ReadResult result = await reader . ReadAsync (); ReadOnlySequence < byte > buffer = result . Buffer ; SequencePosition consumed = buffer . Start ; while ( TryParseMessage ( ref buffer , out Message msg )) { await HandleMessageAsync ( msg ); consumed = buffer . Start ; } // consumed: pipe can reclaim this memory // examined (buffer.End): I've seen everything but no complete message yet - // don't call me again until there's more data reader . AdvanceTo ( consumed , buffer . End ); if ( result . IsCompleted ) break ; } } finally { await reader . CompleteAsync (); } } // Length-prefixed frame parser - no allocations for incomplete frames static bool TryParseMessage ( ref ReadOnlySequence < byte > buffer , out Message message ) { // Need at least 4 bytes for the length prefix if ( buffer . Length < 4 ) { message = default ; return false ; } // Read length prefix without allocating - stack-allocate the 4 bytes Span < byte > lengthBytes = stackalloc byte [ 4 ]; buffer . Slice ( 0 , 4 ). CopyTo ( lengthBytes ); int frameLength = BinaryPrimitives . ReadInt32LittleEndian ( lengthBytes ); // Wait until we have the complete frame if ( buffer . Length < 4 + frameLength ) { message = default ; return false ; } ReadOnlySequence < byte > body = buffer . Slice ( 4 , frameLength ); message = ParseBody ( body ); // parse in-place or copy - your choice buffer = buffer . Slice ( 4 + frameLength ); // advance past this frame return true ; } Backpressure is structural: FlushAsync on the writer blocks when the reader is behind, preventing unbounded memory growth. You don't write this logic yourself - it's in the pipe. System.Threading.Channels - producer-consumer without locks Channel is .NET's built-in producer-consumer queue with async read/write, bounded capacity, and backpressure. The advantage over ConcurrentQueue: channels are async-native and don't require polling. Consumers await new items instead of spinning on TryDequeue in a loop. // Bounded channel - backpressure kicks in when full Channel < WorkItem > channel = Channel . CreateBounded < WorkItem >( new BoundedChannelOptions ( 1000 ) { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode . Wait , // producer awaits space - true backpressure SingleWriter = false , SingleReader = false , }); // Producer - WriteAsync yields when channel is at capacity async Task ProduceAsync ( ChannelWriter < WorkItem > writer , IAsyncEnumerable < WorkItem > source ) { await foreach ( var item in source ) { await writer . WriteAsync ( item ); // blocks if full - backpressure propagates upstream } writer . Complete (); } // Consumer - ReadAllAsync exits cleanly when channel is complete async Task ConsumeAsync ( ChannelReader < WorkItem > reader ) { await foreach ( WorkItem item in reader . ReadAllAsync ()) { await ProcessItemAsync ( item ); } } BoundedChannelFullMode controls what happens when the channel is at capacity. Wait is the right default for services where you want backpressure to propagate - the producer slows down naturally when the consumer can't keep up. DropOldest is useful for telemetry sampling where stale data is less valuable than new data. DropWrite (WriteAsync returns false without blocking) is useful for rate-limiting at ingestion where you want to explicitly account for drops. // Fan-out to multiple consumers - same channel, multiple consumer tasks var channel = Channel . CreateBounded < WorkItem >( 1000 ); // Start N consumers before any producer writes var consumers = Enumerable . Range ( 0 , 8 ) . Select ( _ => ConsumeAsync ( channel . Reader )) . ToArray (); // Multiple producers can write concurrently - channel handles the synchronization var producers = Enumerable . Range ( 0 , 4 ) . Select ( i => ProduceAsync ( channel . Writer , GetBatch ( i ))) . ToArray (); await Task . WhenAll ( producers ); channel . Writer . Complete (); // no more items - consumers will drain and exit await Task . WhenAll ( consumers ); // Use Channel.CreateUnbounded<T>() when: // - The producer is bounded and you control it (DB cursor, file read) // - You need guaranteed delivery and can afford the memory // Don't use it for external input you don't control - OOM under spikes Putting all four together: a log ingestion service Here's what it looks like when these four primitives share a service. A TCP log ingestion endpoint: the socket fills a pipe, the pipe reader parses lines with Span, complete parsed lines go into a channel, and multiple processor workers consume from the channel. public sealed class LogIngestionService : BackgroundService { private readonly Channel < ParsedLogLine > _channel ; private readonly ILogProcessor [] _processors ; public LogIngestionService ( ILogProcessor [] processors ) { _processors = processors ; _channel = Channel . CreateBounded < ParsedLogLine >( new BoundedChannelOptions ( 10_000 ) { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode . Wait , SingleWriter = true , // only the parse loop writes SingleReader = false , // multiple processor workers read }); } protected override async Task ExecuteAsync ( CancellationToken ct ) { var listener = new TcpListener ( IPAddress . Any , 9200 ); listener . Start (); // Consumers start before we accept any connections Task [] consumers = _processors . Select ( p => ConsumeAsync ( p , ct )) . ToArray (); try { while (! ct . IsCancellationRequested ) { TcpClient client = await listener . AcceptTcpClientAsync ( ct ); _ = HandleConnectionAsync ( client , ct ); // fire-and-forget per connection } } finally { _channel . Writer . Complete (); await Task . WhenAll ( consumers ); } } private async Task HandleConnectionAsync ( TcpClient client , CancellationToken ct ) { using var _ = client ; var pipe = new Pipe (); await Task . WhenAll ( FillAsync ( client . GetStream (), pipe . Writer , ct ), ParseAsync ( pipe . Reader , ct ) ); } private static async Task FillAsync ( Stream stream , PipeWriter writer , CancellationToken ct ) { try { while (! ct . IsCancellationRequested ) { Memory < byte > buffer = writer . GetMemory ( 1024 ); int read = await stream . ReadAsync ( buffer , ct ); if ( read == 0 ) break ; writer . Advance ( read ); if (( await writer . FlushAsync ( ct )). IsCompleted ) break ; } } finally { await writer . CompleteAsync (); } } private async Task ParseAsync ( PipeReader reader , CancellationToken ct ) { try { while (! ct . IsCancellationRequested ) { ReadResult result = await reader . ReadAsync ( ct ); ReadOnlySequence < byte > buffer = result . Buffer ; SequencePosition consumed = buffer . Start ; while ( TryReadLine ( ref buffer , out ReadOnlySequence < byte > line )) { // All of this stays on the stack - no heap allocations per line if ( TryParseLine ( line , out ParsedLogLine parsed )) await _channel . Writer . WriteAsync ( parsed , ct ); consumed = buffer . Start ; } reader . AdvanceTo ( consumed , buffer . End ); if ( result . IsCompleted ) break ; } } finally { await reader . CompleteAsync (); } } private static bool TryReadLine ( ref ReadOnlySequence < byte > buffer , out ReadOnlySequence < byte > line ) { SequencePosition ? newline = buffer . PositionOf (( byte ) '\n' ); if ( newline is null ) { line = default ; return false ; } line = buffer . Slice ( 0 , newline . Value ); buffer = buffer . Slice ( buffer . GetPosition ( 1 , newline . Value )); return true ; } private static bool TryParseLine ( ReadOnlySequence < byte > line , out ParsedLogLine parsed ) { if ( line . Length > 2048 ) { parsed = default ; return false ; } // Copy to stack for Span<byte> work - no heap allocation for the working buffer Span < byte > bytes = stackalloc byte [( int ) line . Length ]; line . CopyTo ( bytes ); int firstSpace = bytes . IndexOf (( byte ) ' ' ); if ( firstSpace < 0 ) { parsed = default ; return false ; } ReadOnlySpan < byte > timestampPart = bytes . Slice ( 0 , firstSpace ); ReadOnlySpan < byte > rest = bytes . Slice ( firstSpace + 1 ); parsed = new ParsedLogLine ( Timestamp : ParseTimestamp ( timestampPart ), Raw : line . ToArray () // one allocation - only when we actually need to keep the data ); return true ; } private async Task ConsumeAsync ( ILogProcessor processor , CancellationToken ct ) { await foreach ( ParsedLogLine line in _channel . Reader . ReadAllAsync ( ct )) await processor . ProcessAsync ( line , ct ); } } When not to reach for these Span and Memory add cognitive load. For most service code - request handlers, repository methods, domain logic - allocation overhead is irrelevant and the constraint that Span can't cross the heap is a maintenance burden. Profile before reaching for this. If your flame graph doesn't show GC pressure in that code path, leave it alone. System.IO.Pipelines is specifically for streaming I/O with partial-read framing. If your network reads always return complete messages (HTTP request bodies, short socket commands with a simple delimiter), a Stream with manual buffering is simpler and correct. Pipelines earn their complexity at high connection counts where the partial-read logic is the hard part. Channel is overkill when producer and consumer run at similar rates with no backpressure risk, or when you just need fire-and-forget background work (Task.Run is fine). Use it when you specifically need bounded capacity, graceful shutdown via Complete(), or async awaiting on an empty queue without polling. The question is always the same: does the profiler show allocation pressure or contention in this specific path? These four primitives are the answer to specific, measurable problems. Used speculatively, they're just complexity.

title: Why I Built a Habit Tracker That Refuses to Touch the Cloud
author: Zoe parker
summary: Why I Built a Habit Tracker That Refuses to Touch the Cloud published: true tags: WebDAV, mobile, architecture, privacy Like many developers, I’ve tried dozens of productivities and habit-tracking apps. And like many developers, I eventually grew exhausted by the modern SaaS playbook: Create an account (email, password, verification link). Grant permissions so your local state can live on someone else's server. Deal with cloud synchronization spinners just to check off a daily routine. Get bombarded with push notifications and engagement loops designed to hijack attention. I didn't want a social network for habits. I didn't want my daily routines logged in a remote PostgreSQL database. I just wanted a fast, private tool that stayed entirely on my device. So, I decided to build my own: My Momentum. The Philosophy: Minimalist Engineering & Local-First My Momentum is built on a strict premise: **Your data belongs to you, and your app shouldn't need an internet connection to function. Here is what that looks like in practice: Zero Auth / Zero Onboarding: There is no authentication wall. Users shouldn't have to hand over their email address just to track whether they went for a walk or read a book. You open the app and you're ready to go. Local-First Architecture: All state lives locally on-device using efficient client-side storage (SQLite/Indexed DB depending on the platform layer). No backend database latency, zero server-side maintenance overhead, and complete data ownership. 3.Zero Notification Spam: No intrusive push notification schedulers or dark patterns. Software should serve the user, not hijack their dopamine receptors. Overcoming Technical Constraints Building an offline-first app without cloud sync sounds simple on paper, but it forces you to rethink standard app patterns: State Persistence: Without a server to fall back on, local state management has to be bulletproof. Ensuring atomic writes and graceful error handling locally prevents any corrupted state issues on mobile. Zero-Telemetry Footprint: Skipping third-party analytics SDKs and tracking pixels means faster load times, zero battery drain from background phoning-home, and total user privacy by design. What's Next? I've built out a clean static landing page hosted via Netlify and Vercel to collect early waitlist signups ahead of the public rollout, focusing entirely on a product-led, minimalist approach. If you're building local-first software, working with zero-login architectures, or just tired of everything requiring a cloud backend, I’d love to hear how you handle local state management and persistence in your own projects! title: Best Exchange Rate API for Europe in 2026: 8 Compared for EUR Rates, ECB Reference Rates and VAT
author: Exchange Rate API
summary: For a European business the euro reference rate from the European Central Bank is the default answer to every currency question, and several free APIs serve it. The choice gets harder when you also need a live rate for checkout, a non-euro official rate for a subsidiary in Poland or Switzerland, or output your accounting system can import. This comparison looks at eight exchange rate APIs from the point of view of a team in Europe. Free-tier limits and prices were read from each provider's own pricing page on 10 November 2026; they change often, so confirm before you commit. What a team in Europe needs from an exchange rate API Live EUR pairs for pricing and checkout, not just a daily fixing. ECB euro foreign exchange reference rates , the rate EU VAT rules allow for invoices in other currencies. Other European central banks : Switzerland, Poland, Czechia, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Hungary and the UK each publish their own table. History by date , for the date VAT became chargeable. Monthly averages , which Germany uses for VAT returns. Published for 29 currencies, usually updated at around 16:00 CET every working day, from a concertation at about 14:10 CET. The ECB publishes them for information purposes only. VAT Directive, Article 91(2). The exchange rate is the latest selling rate recorded on the most representative exchange market of the Member State when VAT becomes chargeable. Member States shall accept instead the latest exchange rate published by the European Central Bank at that time. Germany. For VAT returns, section 16(6) of the German VAT Act requires conversion at the monthly average rates announced by the Federal Ministry of Finance, which are monthly averages of the ECB reference rates. Outside the euro area. Each national central bank publishes its own table, and local rules usually name it. A group with entities in several countries needs each bank's table, not a euro cross rate. The point for choosing an API: a market mid-rate and an official table are different products. A market rate is right for showing a customer a price. It is not the figure a tax form or an auditor asks for. The eight providers 1. AllRatesToday Best for: teams that need both kinds of rate. Mid-market rates for 160+ currencies refresh every 60 seconds on every plan, on any base currency, over HTTPS. The same key serves the official tables of 123 central banks and 6 tax authorities, each with the publisher's own date. For Europe that means: ECB reference rates, plus the other European central banks and the Swiss customs table. Output is JSON, CSV, XML or Excel from the same endpoints, with SDKs for JavaScript, Python, PHP, Go and Rust and an MCP server for AI agents. title: One Coding Budget, Multiple Models: Configure Claude Code with the Right Protocol
author: Germey
summary: If you already use terminal coding agents but do not want separate subscriptions and credentials for every model family, AceDataCloud Coding Plan is designed for that workflow. The current public catalog starts with Coding Plus at a ¥99 CNY display anchor (US$14.645677), valid for 30 days , with 400 base Credits plus a 100-Credit limited-time bonus through November 30, 2026 (UTC+8) . It is a metered multi-model API plan—not an official Claude, ChatGPT, or Codex membership, and not unlimited usage. This guide shows how to choose the correct protocol, configure Claude Code safely, verify the connection, and allocate a fixed Credit budget across real development tasks. Start with the protocol, not the model name Coding clients do not all speak the same API protocol. Picking a model family first and forcing it into an incompatible client creates avoidable configuration failures. Coding Plan currently exposes three useful interface patterns: Workflow Interface Typical clients Anthropic-native agent workflow Claude Messages Claude Code OpenAI agent workflow OpenAI Responses Codex Custom-provider workflow OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions Kimi Code, OpenClaw, OpenCode, Cline, Aider, and others The plan covers model ecosystems including Claude, GPT/Codex, GLM, Kimi, and DeepSeek. However, that does not mean every client supports every model or protocol. Check the live model directory, credential scope, and the integration guide for your chosen client before committing a project to a combination. A practical rule is: Keep the client that already fits your workflow. Select the protocol that client expects. Choose an available model for the task. Verify one read-only request before allowing edits or tool execution. Minimal Claude Code configuration First, purchase a Coding Plan, create a Coding Application, and copy its dedicated API key from the application console. Coding Applications do not fall back to your general platform balance, which keeps this workload inside its defined budget. Install Claude Code on macOS, Linux, or WSL: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash claude --version Then configure the Anthropic-compatible endpoint. For global use, add these lines to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc : export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL = "https://api.acedata.cloud" export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "YOUR_CODING_APPLICATION_KEY" unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Reload the shell: source ~/.zshrc # or: source ~/.bashrc For project-only configuration, use .claude/settings.local.json instead: { "env" : { "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL" : "https://api.acedata.cloud" , "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN" : "YOUR_CODING_APPLICATION_KEY" } } Add that local settings file to .gitignore . Do not put a real key in the team-shared .claude/settings.json , and do not leave a conflicting ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment. Verify before granting write access Start in a repository with a small, read-only request: cd /path/to/your/project claude Then ask: Read README.md and summarize the project in one sentence. Do not modify files. A successful answer confirms that the client launches and the request reaches a model, but complete verification should include four checks: the response matches the repository content; no file changed ( git status --short is empty); a call appears in AceDataCloud Usage History; the Coding Application balance decreases as expected. If you receive 401 , verify that the key is complete, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is genuinely unset, and the terminal plus Claude Code have been fully restarted. If a model is missing, refresh the model directory and check its exact ID against the credential's API scope and client protocol. Allocate models by task, not habit A multi-model plan is most useful when model choice follows task risk and context size. A simple allocation policy is: Task Selection priority Validation README, comments, boilerplate tests Lower-cost capable model Lint and test output Cross-file bug investigation Strong code understanding and context handling Reproduce before and after Architecture or security review Strong reasoning model Human review plus independent checks Repetitive migration work Reliable tool-use loop Small batch, diff review, then expand This is not a claim that one model family is universally best. It is a way to avoid spending premium-model Credits on low-risk work while still reserving stronger reasoning for expensive mistakes. Budget with Credits correctly All four current tiers have the same Coding model access; they mainly differ in included Credits. Coding Plus currently includes 500 promotional Credits (400 base plus 100 bonus) for 30 days. Usage is not measured as a fixed number of prompts: uncached input, output, cache writes, and cache reads are metered separately. Long context, parallel agents, tool loops, and verbose output can all increase consumption. For a first month, set three guardrails: Start with one repository and one client. This makes usage attributable. Measure representative tasks. Run a test-generation task, a cross-file fix, and a review; record Credits consumed by each. Set a stop threshold. At 70–80% of the quota, review usage before starting long agent loops. Renewing before expiry carries remaining Credits forward and extends validity by 30 days. If the plan expires without renewal, unused Credits expire; plans do not auto-renew. When this setup is a good fit Coding Plan is a reasonable option when you want to keep Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code, OpenClaw, or another compatible client while choosing among multiple model ecosystems under one time-limited API budget. It is less compelling if one existing single-model plan already covers all your work, or if you need unlimited usage. Review the current plans and purchase entry and use the Coding Plan Setup Center to select the guide that matches your client. title: Why Duplicate Training Data Silently Corrupts Vision Models
author: Harpreet Sahota
summary: What is worse than bad training data? Duplicate training data that silently corrupts your model while convincing you that performance is flawless. Every duplicate and near-duplicate image in your dataset amplifies sampling bias, wastes compute, and forces your model to overfit. Most dangerously, traditional validation metrics will not warn you. When near-identical frames exist across both your training and validation splits, evaluation metrics measure memorization rather than generalization. The result is an artificial spike in precision-recall curves, inflated mean average precision (mAP), and high confidence scores that unravel the moment the model encounters the real world. To prevent this silent failure, engineering teams must implement strategic, cluster-aware dataset pruning. +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ | THE IMPACT OF DUPLICATE DATA ON VISION MODELS | +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ [Train-Val Leakage] --> Inflated validation metrics (false mAP) [Loss Imbalance] --> Gradient updates over-index on duplicates [Diversity Loss] --> Representation collapses to oversampled modes +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ | STRATEGIC PRUNING STEPS | +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ 1. Cryptographic check for bitwise exact duplicates (MD5/SHA) 2. Embedding similarity clustering for near-duplicate sets 3. Selective pruning: preserve rare angles, remove redundancy +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ The Anatomy of Silent Corruption When video streams or burst captures are sampled without adequate temporal spacing, consecutive frames capture essentially identical geometry, lighting, and object postures. This causes three distinct structural failures: Precision-Recall Curve Distortion: When evaluating object detectors, predictions on memorized duplicate frames yield high-confidence true positives with zero localization error. These easy hits artificially inflate the area under the PR curve, masking severe failure modes on novel, diverse test samples. Feature Representation Collapse: In self-supervised and supervised representation learning, gradient updates are dominated by the most frequent visual patterns. If 20% of your dataset consists of near-identical frames of an empty warehouse aisle, the model allocates disproportionate representational capacity to that specific background. Overconfidence on Minor Variations: Models trained on redundant data fail to learn invariance to physical camera motion. Instead of learning that a forklift remains a forklift across continuous viewing angles, the model memorizes specific pixel configurations. Exact Duplicates vs. Semantic Near-Duplicates Deduplication requires two complementary detection strategies: 1. Exact Bitwise Duplicates These are identical files or duplicate frame exports. They can be detected in linear time using cryptographic hashing: import hashlib from pathlib import Path def find_exact_duplicates ( image_paths ) : hashes = { } duplicates = [ ] for path in image_paths : hasher = hashlib . md5 ( ) with open ( path , "rb" ) as f : hasher . update ( f . read ( ) ) digest = hasher . hexdigest ( ) if digest in hashes : duplicates . append ( ( path , hashes [ digest ] ) ) else : hashes [ digest ] = path return duplicates Exact bitwise duplicates should be pruned immediately without hesitation. 2. Semantic Near-Duplicates Near-duplicates share the same physical scene but vary slightly in camera position, minor illumination changes, compression artifacts, or subtle foreground movement. Cryptographic hashes fail completely on these samples. Detecting near-duplicates requires computing pairwise cosine similarity across dense feature embeddings: $$\text{Sim}(u, v) = \frac{u \cdot v}{|u| |v|}$$ Using FiftyOne, you can identify and group near-duplicate clusters efficiently: import fiftyone as fo import fiftyone . brain as fob dataset = fo . load_dataset ( "surveillance_feed_raw" ) # Index embeddings for similarity search fob . compute_similarity ( dataset , model = "clip-vit-base32-torch" , brain_key = "img_sim" ) # Find near-duplicate pairs with cosine similarity > 0.98 duplicate_map = fob . find_duplicates ( dataset , similarity_threshold = 0.98 , brain_key = "img_sim" ) print ( f "Identified {len(duplicate_map)} near-duplicate groups." ) The Trap of Blind Deduplication: Why Selective Pruning Matters A common operational error is running an automated script that deletes all but one frame from every near-duplicate cluster. Blind pruning frequently destroys valuable edge cases: In continuous video, an object transition (e.g. an assembly line component shifting alignment or a pedestrian starting to cross) may occur within a near-duplicate sequence. Near-duplicate sequences often contain subtle lighting variations or extreme camera angles that provide valuable regularization. Strategic Pruning Rules Follow a disciplined three-phase pruning protocol: Prune exact duplicates first: Remove identical files and verify that no sample ID exists in both training and test splits. Cluster near-duplicates: Group samples with similarity $> 0.96$ into explicit equivalence classes. Apply diversity-preserving selection: Within each near-duplicate cluster, select representatives that maximize visual diversity (e.g., the frame with the highest contrast, the sharpest focus, or the most extreme viewing angle) and prune the redundant interior frames. Deduplication Stage Target Similarity Detection Method Preservation Rule Exact Clones $1.00$ bitwise MD5 / SHA-256 Hashing Purge completely Near Clones $> 0.985$ cosine Embedding similarity Keep 1 representative per burst Semantic Siblings $0.94 - 0.98$ cosine Clustering (DBSCAN/k-NN) Select frames with diverse angles/lighting Distinct Scenes $< 0.90$ cosine Baseline distribution Preserve all valid instances Building Reliable Production Datasets Eliminating redundant duplicates restores integrity to your evaluation splits, ensures that gradient updates reflect genuine visual variance, and cuts training time without sacrificing performance. For companion reading on dataset curation and evaluation, see our articles on finding edited copies with pHash and FiftyOne and evaluating AI agent pipelines . To master hands-on dataset curation and pruning workflows, audit Harpreet Sahota's Coursera course: Hands-on Data Centric Visual AI . Frequently asked questions How do duplicate images cause train-test data leakage? When identical or near-duplicate frames appear in both training and test splits, the model is evaluated on samples it has already memorized. This creates artificially inflated validation metrics that collapse upon live deployment. Why does duplicate data inflate mean average precision (mAP)? Duplicates create artificial clusters in high-confidence regions of precision-recall curves. The model repeatedly scores easy True Positives on memorized duplicate samples, lifting aggregate area under the curve despite poor generalization on novel images. What is the difference between exact duplicates and near-duplicates? Exact duplicates have identical pixel values and can be detected using MD5 or SHA-256 hashes. Near-duplicates share identical scenes with minor variations in crop, lighting, compression, or sensor angle, requiring perceptual hashing or embedding cosine distance to detect. How can teams implement selective dataset pruning?
