title: Muse Ember at $0.10/$0.50: Default Is Max, the 200K Billing Cliff, and When to Pair It With Wonder
author: Yong Yu
summary: Attributed compile + list-price arithmetic on my box Primary source: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember (Nov 9, 2026) by Meta AI Research . Docs: Muse Ember , Choose a model , Reasoning , Pricing and rate limits . Independent index scrape: Artificial Analysis — Muse Ember (Max) ( intelligenceIndex ≈ 36.02 , isOpenWeights: false ); Muse Ember (xhigh) (≈ 34.11 ). Routing / list prices: OpenRouter: meta/muse-ember (canonical slug meta/muse-ember-20261109 ). Discussion (not a source of numbers): HN: Muse Ember (~318 points / 137 comments at check). Local copies: /workspace/reputation/runs/38-muse-ember/ . Numbers below from the announcement, Meta docs, AA scrape, or OpenRouter's models API are vendor / dashboard unless marked otherwise. This box did not hold a Meta or OpenRouter key and did not send a chat completion. The only local run is list-price arithmetic in cliff.py . Meta released Muse Ember on 2026-11-09 as the cheap workhorse in the Muse lineup: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, and the other loops agents repeat all day. On Meta Model API and in Muse Code the id is muse-ember-1.0 . Under the 200K-input line, list price is $0.10 / $0.004 cached / $0.50 per 1M tokens — and the default reasoning effort is max . Those two facts, not the efficiency chart, are what will surprise you on the first invoice. If you already use Muse Wonder for hard problems and Muse Spark (including Spark Open weights) for the mid-tier loop, Ember is the volume lane: a larger model plans, Ember runs the bounded work. It is not open-weights — Artificial Analysis still has isOpenWeights: false and no parameter count. What matters on day one is how you call it, what the 200K full-request cliff does to a bill, why you must set reasoning_effort yourself, and when to stay on Spark or Wonder. What shipped Vendor docs and the announcement, compressed: Field Value Model ID muse-ember-1.0 Inputs → output Text, image, video, audio, and PDF → text Context / max output 1,048,576 / 524,288 tokens Reasoning "minimal" through "max" ; default "max" ; "none" returns HTTP 400 Endpoints Responses, Chat Completions, Messages Mode on Model API Standard only (no Contributor-mode variant) Rate limits (docs) 3,000 RPM / 4,000,000 TPM, per team License Proprietary / hosted. Weights are not public. Surfaces Model API; Muse Code (pay-as-you-go and every plan). The announcement also names Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud. Meta's positioning, paraphrased: Ember is the first model trained using Muse Wonder Full, and it rounds out the portfolio — Wonder for the hardest problems, Spark for coding and agentic workflows, Ember for repeatable tasks at a cost they quote as about $0.14 per Artificial Analysis task. This box opened those pages, plus OpenRouter and the HN Firebase item (318 points / 137 comments at check) — all HTTP 200 . No Meta or OpenRouter key, so no completion was sent. OpenRouter's pin is meta/muse-ember (canonical slug meta/muse-ember-20261109 ); their models API matched Meta's $0.10 / $0.50 and cache-read $0.004 , and also listed a cache-write of $0.125 per 1M that Meta's pricing table does not show as a separate line. A Responses call should pin the model and set effort plus an output cap. The first two fields follow Meta's first-call snippet; reasoning.effort and max_output_tokens are what the reasoning docs say you need, not something I measured: curl -X POST "https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $MODEL_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "muse-ember-1.0", "input": "Classify this support ticket as billing, bug, or feature request, and give a one-sentence reason: \"I was charged twice for my October invoice.\"", "reasoning": { "effort": "medium" }, "max_output_tokens": 2048 }' On Chat Completions the same knob is top-level reasoning_effort . Pricing and the 200K cliff From Meta's pricing doc, Ember has two tiers, and the input token count in the request — cached tokens included — picks the tier for the entire request . A stored conversation continued with previous_response_id counts that history as input. Cross 200K and you pay long-context rates in full, not only for the tokens past 200K . Usage (USD per 1M tokens) Up to 200K input Over 200K input Cached input $0.004 $0.012 Input $0.10 $0.30 Output $0.50 $1.50 Cache read is 4% of the uncached input rate on both tiers. Wonder and Spark have no long-context premium: Wonder Standard is $4.00 / $0.20 cached / $20.00 , and Spark 1.3 Standard is $1.25 / $0.15 cached / $4.25 . Ember is Standard-only; Contributor discounts exist for Spark, not Ember. Web search grounding on the web_search tool is an extra $2.50 per 1,000 queries. I ran cliff.py on those list prices (arithmetic, not an API invoice): subagent 8,000 in + 1,500 out, 0% cache, short: $0.001550 same call, 80% cache hit, short: $0.000936 199,000 in + 2,000 out, 0% cache, short: $0.020900 201,000 in + 2,000 out, 0% cache, long: $0.063300 ratio: 3.03x for ~1% more input 199,000 in + 2,000 out, 90% cache, short: $0.003706 201,000 in + 2,000 out, 90% cache, long: $0.011201 ratio: 3.02x Spark 1.3 Standard, 201k+2k, 0% cache: $0.259750 Wonder 1.0 Standard, 201k+2k, 0% cache: $0.844000 Stuffing a conversation or repo just over 200K roughly triples that Ember call versus staying under the line. Even after the flip, the same 201K+2K tokens are still cheaper on Ember's long tier than on Spark or Wonder at Standard list prices — the cliff is versus Ember's own cheap band, not a reason to assume Spark is cheaper for long prompts. If you need flat long-context pricing and harder single-shot coding, Spark or Wonder are the capability upgrade. On a Muse Code subscription, docs say a request over 200K input also burns plan usage faster. Default is max, and none is a 400 Wonder, Spark, and Ember generate internal reasoning that stays out of the response body, but those tokens count toward max_tokens / max_output_tokens and billed output. If most of the budget goes to reasoning, the visible answer can truncate. The effort ladder is minimal , low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . "none" is not supported and returns HTTP 400 . When you omit the parameter, Wonder and Ember default to max ; Spark defaults to high . Meta describes max as going beyond xhigh : more reasoning tokens, same per-token price. That is the other invoice surprise. A "cheap subagent" call with no effort set is a max call. Set the knob on every request, pick the lowest level that works for that subtask, and set the output cap high enough for reasoning plus visible text. Log completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens or the Responses equivalent. This box did not measure token splits or latency. Short score map (vendor + AA — not our eval) Meta's announcement table, all models at max , AA Intelligence Index v5 as published November 9, 2026, Ember costs at list pricing: Bench Muse Ember (max) Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) GPT-6 Luna (max) AA Intelligence Index 36 36 28 AutomationBench-AA (strict pass@1) 37.8% 13.9% 20.2% Terminal-Bench 4.0 (best published harness) 40.9% 39.2% 16.4% Coding Agent Index-AA 46 37 31 FrontierCode 2.0-AA 27.2% 34.9% 25.2% GDP.pdf-AA 22.8% 20.8% 22.8% Meta's footnote: Terminal-Bench 4.0 used mini-swe-agent for Ember, Claude Code for Haiku 5.5, and Codex for Luna — not a same-harness bake-off. Our AA.com scrape on 2026-11-10 for Muse Ember (Max): index ≈ 36.02 , cost per index task ≈ $0.135 (headline $0.14 ), time-per-task headline 3.2 minutes , time to first answer token 4.37s , output speed 446 tok/s , FrontierCode 2.0 ≈ 27.2% , Terminal-Bench 4.0 ≈ 40.9% , GDP.pdf all-pass 22.8% . The xhigh index was ≈ 34.11 . In the same scrape, Haiku 5.5 was ≈ 36.48 and Luna ≈ 27.86 — in line with Meta's rounded 36 / 28, with Haiku a hair ahead unrounded. The honest coding caveat is FrontierCode 2.0 : Haiku 5.5 leads in the announcement table (34.9 vs 27.2), and our scrape of Ember max matches that 27.2. Meta's own "choose a model" page says to use Spark or Wonder for hard single-shot coding, knowledge-heavy questions, or visual coding. Treat Ember as a volume executor , not a drop-in for merge-quality work. The announcement also compares Ember (max) with Spark 1.3 (max): AA Index 36 vs 37 , cost per AA task $0.14 vs $2.39 , list $0.10/$0.50 vs $1.25/$4.25 — vendor figures, not a run from this box. When to use Ember vs Spark vs Wonder Ember when a larger model plans and sub-agents run many bounded tasks: classification, extraction, tool calls, terminal subtasks, or the same job over a pile of files or tickets. Keep prompts under 200K input for the cheap band. If a session grows past that line, summarize or truncate before the flip, or move the long-horizon pass to Spark or Wonder. Spark ( muse-spark-1.3 is the recommended id) for the main agent loop, or harder work at a lower cost than Wonder. Pricing is flat at any context length. Contributor-mode ids exist if you accept training on your content; Ember does not have that option. Wonder ( muse-wonder-1.0 ) when capability matters more than cost. Long-context pricing is also flat. Wonder Full is Muse Code only — there is no Model API id for it. Pairing is a model-id change on the same request body. Pin muse-ember-1.0 (or OpenRouter meta/muse-ember ), set effort yourself, watch input size including cache and conversation history , and escalate hard merge work. Ember is hosted-only; weights still mean the Spark Open path. For a Toronto product team on 2026-11-10 , the rational first move is pin the id, set effort below max, keep input under the 200K line, and put Ember behind a planner — not to paste a whole repo into one call and then wonder why the bill jumped 3×. title: The most expensive token is the one you spend twice
author: Jonathan Berg
summary: Everyone building with AI watches token prices. New model comes out, the first thing we check is the cost per million. We negotiate with ourselves over which tier a task deserves. Meanwhile the biggest line item on the bill goes completely unmeasured: the work your agent does again because it forgot it already did it. Think about what happens in a typical session. The agent re-reads your project. Re-learns your conventions. Rebuilds a component that already exists somewhere in your history, slightly worse this time. It is like a chef who walks into the kitchen and has to forge the knives, build the stove and carve the cutting board before cooking every single meal. The cooking is the part that matters. Most of the compute goes into remaking tools that were already made. The waste is structural This is not a model problem, and a better model will not fix it. A smarter agent with no memory still starts every session from zero. It will be brilliantly, expensively ignorant. It will derive the same conventions, rediscover the same edge cases, and rewrite the same code, at a higher price per token than the model you had last year. We have built an entire industry on top of amnesia and learned to call the repeated reasoning intelligence. When an agent re-explains your own codebase back to you, it feels like understanding. It is actually the meter running. Memory is a compute optimization Once you see the waste, memory stops looking like a convenience feature. It is infrastructure. Every time an agent fetches a proven component, a saved method or a known answer instead of regenerating one, that is compute you do not spend. The hard thinking happens once, and the repeats get cheap. Cheap enough, often, that a smaller model can run them, because following saved work takes less than inventing it. This reframing changed how I think about what I am building with Sirro. I used to describe it as a memory layer with a nice side effect on cost. That is backwards. The cost is the point. Memory just happens to be the mechanism that gets you there. The kitchen where the tools stay on the wall is not a comfort. It is the difference between cooking and reforging. The honest metric So here is the number I actually care about now, and it is not on any pricing page. How much of what your agent did this week had already been done before? Every rebuild is a choice you paid for, made quietly by a system that cannot remember. Tokens spent learning something new are an investment. Tokens spent relearning something old are a leak. If your agent rebuilt work this week that already existed, you did not pay for intelligence. You paid for forgetting.
